translations.note: Title of Burton's own Latin verses addressed to his book.

ad-librum-f2.text: Vade liber, qualis, non ausum dicere, foelix, / Te nisi foelicem fecerit Alma dies. / Vade tamen quocunque lubet, quascunque per oras, / Et Genium Domini fac imitere tui. / I blandas inter Charites, mystamque saluta / Musarum quemvis, si tibi lector erit. / Rura colas, urbem, subeasve palatia regum, / Submisse, placide, te sine dente geras. / Nobilis, aut si quis te forte inspexerit heros, / Da te morigerum, perlegat usque lubet. / Est quod Nobilitas, est quod desideret heros, / Gratior haec forsan charta placere potest. / Si quis morosus Cato, tetricusque Senator, / Hunc etiam librum forte videre velit, / Sive magistratus, tum te reverenter habeto; / Sed nullus; muscas non capiunt Aquilae. / Non vacat his tempus fugitivum impendere nugis, / Nec tales cupio, par mihi lector erit. / Si matrona gravis casu diverterit istuc, / Illustris domina, aut te Comitissa legat: / Est quod displiceat, placeat quod forsitan illis, / Ingerere his noli te modo, pande tamen. / At si virgo tuas dignabitur inclyta chartas / Tangere, sive schedis haereat illa tuis: / Da modo te facilem, & quaedam folia esse memento / Conveniant oculis quae magis apta suis. / Si generosa ancilla tuos aut alma puella / Visura est ludos, annue, pande lubens. / Dic utinam nunc ipse meus (nam diligit istas) / In praesens esset conspiciendus herus. / Ignotus notusve mihi de gente togata / Sive aget in ludis, pulpita sive colet, / Sive in Lycaeo, & nugas evolverit istas, / Si quasdam mendas viderit inspiciens, / Da veniam Authori, dices; nam plurima vellet / Expungi, quae jam displicuisse sciat. / Sive Melancholicus quisquam, seu blandus Amator, / Aulicus aut Civis, seu bene comptus Eques / Huc appellat, age & tuto te crede legenti, / Multa istic forsan non male nata leget. / Quod fugiat, caveat, quodque amplexabitur, ista / Pagina fortassis promere multa potest. / At si quis Medicus coram te sistet, amice / Fac circumspecte, & te sine labe geras: / Inveniet namque ipse meis quoque plurima scriptis, / Non leve subsidium quae sibi forsan erunt. / Si quis Causidicus chartas impingat in istas, / Nil mihi vobiscum, pessima turba vale; / Sit nisi vir bonus, & juris sine fraude peritus, / Tum legat, & forsan doctior inde siet. / Si quis cordatus, facilis, lectorque benignus / Huc oculos vertat, quae velit ipse legat; / Candidus ignoscet, metuas nil, pande libenter, / Offensus mendis non erit ille tuis, / Laudabit nonnulla. Venit si Rhetor ineptus, / Limata & tersa, & qui bene cocta petit, / Claude citus librum; nulla hic nisi ferrea verba, / Offendent stomachum quae minus apta suum. / At si quis non eximius de plebe poeta, / Annue; namque istic plurima ficta leget. / Nos sumus e numero, nullus mihi spirat Apollo, / Grandiloquus Vates quilibet esse nequit. / Si Criticus Lector, tumidus Censorque molestus, / Zoilus & Momus, si rabiosa cohors: / Ringe, freme, & noli tum pandere, turba malignis / Si occurrat sannis invidiosa suis: / Fac fugias; si nulla tibi sit copia eundi, / Contemnes, tacite scommata quaeque feres. / Frendeat, allatret, vacuas gannitibus auras / Impleat, haud cures, his placuisse nefas. / Verum age si forsan divertat purior hospes, / Cuique sales, ludi, displiceantque joci, / Objiciatque tibi sordes, lascivaque: dices, / Lasciva est Domino & Musa jocosa tuo, / Nec lasciva tamen, si pensitet omne; sed esto; / Sit lasciva licet pagina, vita proba est. / Barbarus, indoctusque rudis spectator in istam / Si messem intrudat, fuste fugabis eum, / Fungum pelle procul (jubeo) nam quid mihi fungo? / Conveniunt stomacho non minus ista suo. / Sed nec pelle tamen; laeto omnes accipe vultu, / Quos, quas, vel quales, inde vel unde viros. / Gratus erit quicunque venit, gratissimus hospes / Quisquis erit, facilis difficilisque mihi. / Nam si culparit, quaedam culpasse juvabit, / Culpando faciet me meliora sequi. / Sed si laudarit, neque laudibus efferar ullis, / Sit satis hisce malis opposuisse bonum. / Haec sunt quae nostro placuit mandare libello, / Et quae dimittens dicere jussit Herus.

translations.note: Burton's own Latin verses to his book; the sidenote 'Haec comice dicta cave ne male capias' means 'Take care not to misconstrue what is said here in jest.' 'Fungus' (mushroom) is the usual Latin insult for a dolt, here rendered 'blockhead'. The line 'Conveniunt stomacho non minus ista suo' is ambiguous: literally 'these things suit his stomach no less'. It probably means the book agrees no better with the boor than with the rhetorician, though it could mean the opposite, which would lead into the next line, 'yet do not drive him away'. Hence medium confidence. 'Sit lasciva licet pagina, vita proba est' echoes Martial 1.4.8, 'lasciva est nobis pagina, vita proba.' The opening address to the book follows the classical convention of Ovid (Tristia 1.1) and Martial.
translations.text: Go, book: I would not dare to call you happy, such as you are, / unless a kindly day has made you happy. / Go nevertheless wherever you please, through whatever regions, / and be sure to copy your master's temper. / Go among the charming Graces, and greet any initiate / of the Muses, if he is to be your reader. / Whether you live in the country or the town, or enter the palaces of kings, / bear yourself humbly and quietly, without biting. / If a nobleman, or some hero, should chance to look into you, / show yourself obliging; let him read you through if he pleases. / There is something here that nobility, something that a hero may want; / this page may perhaps give the more pleasure. / If some peevish Cato or stern Senator / should perhaps wish to look at this book too, / or a magistrate, then bear yourself with reverence; / but none will: eagles do not catch flies. / They have no leisure to spend fleeting time on trifles, / nor do I want such readers; my reader shall be my equal. / If a grave matron should chance to turn aside this way, / a noble lady, or a Countess read you: / there is what may displease them, and what perhaps may please them; / only do not thrust yourself on them, yet lie open. / But if a renowned maiden deigns to touch your pages, / or lingers over your leaves: / only make yourself easy, and remember that there are certain leaves / better suited to her eyes. / If a well-born waiting-maid or a kindly girl / is going to look at your sports, nod assent and open gladly. / Say: would that my master himself (for he loves such girls) / were here at this moment to be seen. / If one of the gowned tribe, known or unknown to me, / whether he teaches in the schools or serves the pulpit, / or is in the Lyceum, should unroll these trifles, / and in looking should see some faults, / you will say, Pardon the author, for he would like a great many things / struck out which he knows by now have given displeasure. / Whether some melancholic, or a fond lover, / a courtier or a citizen, or a well-dressed knight / puts in here, come, and trust yourself safely to the reader; / perhaps he will read many things here not ill-born. / What to flee, what to beware of, and what to embrace, this / page can perhaps set forth in plenty. / But if a physician stands before you, my friend, / act with circumspection and bear yourself without blemish: / for he too will find in my writings a great many things / that will perhaps be no slight help to him. / If some pleader should stumble on these pages, / I have nothing to do with you; farewell, you worst of crews; / unless he be a good man, and skilled in the law without fraud: / then let him read, and perhaps be the wiser for it. / If some sensible, easy and kindly reader / turns his eyes this way, let him read what he will; / being candid he will forgive; fear nothing, open freely; / he will not be offended by your faults; / he will praise some things. If a foolish rhetorician comes, / one who looks for things filed and polished and well cooked, / shut the book quickly; there is nothing here but iron words, / which, being ill-suited, will offend his stomach. / But if some undistinguished poet of the common herd comes, / nod assent; for he will read a great many fictions here. / I am one of their number; no Apollo breathes in me; / not everyone can be a grand-voiced bard. / If a critical reader, a swollen and troublesome censor, / a Zoilus and a Momus, if a rabid crew comes: / snarl, growl, and then do not open; if the envious mob / should meet you with their spiteful sneers, / be sure to flee; if you have no means of getting away, / you will despise them and bear every gibe in silence. / Let him gnash his teeth, bark at you, fill the empty air / with yelping; do not care; to have pleased such men would be a sin. / But come, if perhaps a more strait-laced guest should turn in, / one whom witticisms, sports and jests displease, / and he should charge you with filth and wantonness, you will say: / My master's Muse is wanton and jocose, / yet not wanton, if he weighs it all; but be it so: / though the page be wanton, the life is upright. / If a barbarous, unlearned, boorish onlooker / intrudes upon this harvest, you shall drive him off with a cudgel; / drive the blockhead far away (I command it), for what have I to do with a blockhead? / These things suit his stomach no better. / Yet do not drive him away after all; receive everyone with a cheerful face, / men or women, of whatever sort, from here or from anywhere. / Whoever comes will be welcome; the most welcome guest / will be anyone, whether easy or hard to please. / For if he finds fault, it will do good that he has faulted some things; / by finding fault he will make me pursue better things. / But if he praises, I shall not be puffed up by any praises; / let it be enough to have set some good against these ills. / These are the things it pleased me to entrust to my little book, / and which its master, sending it off, bade it say.

ad-librum-f3.text: Haec comice dicta cave ne male capias

translations.literal: These things comically said, beware lest you take badly.
translations.note: Burton's sidenote to his Latin poem 'Ad librum suum' (To his book). It is attached to the parenthesis 'nam diligit istas' ('for he loves them', meaning the noble girls who may read the book). The note asks the reader not to take the playful claim that the author loves women in the wrong way. 'Comice' literally means 'in the manner of comedy'.
translations.text: Take care not to take amiss these things said in jest.
